turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - alloy_pair_constrained_train.csv: 300 samples described by composition in wt% — C, Mn, Si, Cr, Ni, Mo, V, Nb, Co, Al, Ti, Cu
      (Fe is the balance: Fe = 100 − Σ of the others) — plus processing parameters
      (solutionizing_temp, aging_temp, aging_time, cooling_rate) and categorical
      settings heat_treatment (annealed | quenched | quench_temper | solution_aged)
      and route (cast | wrought | AM), with the measured 0.2 % proof yield strength in MPa (the `target` column).
  - alloy_pair_constrained_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE recipes whose yield strength was NOT measured, with the same columns plus `candidate_id` and no `target`.

Both of these hard constraints apply to every candidate:
  1. molybdenum content at most 3.21 wt%;
  2. alloying cost index Σ (price_e × wt%_e) at most 450, using the prices in USD/kg: C 0.5, Mn 2, Si 2.2, Cr 9, Ni 17, Mo 25, V 30, Nb 45, Co 33, Al 2.4, Ti 12, Cu 9.
A candidate that violates either constraint is worth zero, so picking one wastes a slot. Using the training data, predict which FEASIBLE candidates have the HIGHEST yield strength (MPa), then select the 5 best candidates from the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning from the training data

**1. What drives strength?**

Fitting/segmenting the 300 training rows shows that composition effects are dominated by a **Co–Ni pair (maraging‑type) synergy**, not by either element alone:

| group (train) | mean target |
|---|---|
| Co ≈ 7, Ni < 1 (Co alone) | ≈ 1630 MPa |
| Co < 0.5, Ni ≈ 12–20 (Ni alone) | ≈ 1490 MPa |
| Co ≈ 5–7 **and** Ni ≈ 4–9 (both) | ≈ 1970 MPa (top rows 2000–2400) |
| Co ≈ 0, Ni ≈ 0 | ≈ 1400 MPa |

A simple surrogate `≈1350 + 30·Co + 7·Ni + 60·min(Co,Ni) + 20·Mo` reproduces the trend well (e.g. Co 4.85/Ni 8.98 → pred 1900, actual 1918).

**2. Processing offsets** (group means): heat treatment `quench_temper ≈ +120`, `solution_aged ≈ 0`, `quenched ≈ −35`, `annealed ≈ −130`; route `wrought ≈ +60`, `cast ≈ −25`, `AM ≈ −65`. Solutionizing temperature is mildly positive; aging temperature/time and cooling rate show almost no systematic effect. Cr, C, Cu, V are weak; Cr ≥ 18 wt% is slightly detrimental (and expensive).

**3. Feasibility screen** (Mo ≤ 3.21 and cost ≤ 450) knocks out most of the very high‑Co recipes — e.g. c086 (cost 639), c099 (576), c045 (551), c037 (494), c065 (480), c015 (469), c057 (458), c021 (469), c006 (475), c052 (457) — plus Mo violators c030, c049, c055 (3.22), c058, c059.

**4. Best feasible predictions**

| cand | Co / Ni / Mo | HT / route | cost | pred (MPa) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| c007 | 5.26 / 10.24 / 0 | quench_temper, wrought | 411 | ≈ 2030 |
| c044 | 4.72 / 6.49 / 0.95 | quench_temper, cast (Tsol 1228) | 387 | ≈ 1955 |
| c082 | 4.45 / 8.20 / 0.89 | solution_aged, wrought (Tsol 1250) | 388 | ≈ 1925 |
| c029 | 4.86 / 9.04 / 0.66 | quenched, wrought | 421 | ≈ 1900 |
| c064 | 6.08 / 6.27 / 1.31 | annealed, wrought | 421 | ≈ 1900 |
| c003 | 4.38 / 7.51 / 0 | quench_temper, cast | 334 | ≈ 1870 |
| c051 | 3.43 / 13.23 / 0.06 | quench_temper, cast | 371 | ≈ 1805 |

High‑Co but Ni‑starved candidates (c092, c095, c019, c023, c016) score lower because the Co–Ni synergy is missing, matching training rows like Co 8.1/Ni 0.1 → 1487 MPa.

**Final: c007, c044, c082, c029, c064**
